<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-structured cases, but B's rebuttal work was more damaging and more resilient across rounds. B's turn on A's own cluster-munitions analogy (pointing out that the major military powers never signed and used cluster munitions in the very conflict being discussed) was a decisive, factually grounded counter-punch that A never recovered from beyond a hand-wavy "stigma still constrains" assertion. B's pressure question forced A into a concrete, useful definition of "meaningful human control," but B then used that same definition to show the ban either bites on very little (broad reading) or forecloses exactly the prospective, uncertain cases where machines might outperform humans (narrow reading) — a squeeze A's closing acknowledged but didn't fully dissolve. Crucially, B's final rebuttal drew a sharp, undamaged distinction between unilateral regulation (which improves outcomes regardless of adversary compliance) and unilateral prohibition (which only disadvantages the complier) — a point A's closing never directly answered. A did land real hits, especially the pressure question exposing that B's "civilians die from bans" harm was purely prospective, and A's "prevention vs. litigation" framing was clean and memorable. But B answered that concession honestly without collapsing its case, and B's cumulative comparative argument (asymmetry + strict liability as a working, unilateral accountability mechanism) proved more resistant to the exchange. B's two clipped speeches are a real execution cost, but the substance that did land was consistently sharper and more grounded than A's recovery attempts.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's turn on the cluster-munitions precedent in Rebuttal 1 — showing the major powers never signed and used the weapon anyway — which converted A's own supporting example into the strongest evidence for B's asymmetry argument and was never adequately answered.</best_rebuttal>
